You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 6 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'Symmetric_SECE': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 2c7f143a90f6).
S1 S pzp n1 ctrl=G1
S2 S pzn n1 ctrl=G2
L1 L n1 n2 0.002
D1 D n2 out DSCH
G1 SYNC ton=2e-05s phase=0 edges=pos
G2 SYNC ton=2e-05s phase=0 edges=neg
Cout C out 0 4.7e-06
DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: -1.81 uW of 21.6 uW needed (-8 %); S4: -1.81 uW of 3.24 uW needed (-56 %); S6: -1.81 uW of 9.82 uW needed (-18 %)
what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -8 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -56 % of the load's need on S4 (weak excitation), -18 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   `vavg >= 1.8 V` (S1-S6)
        *   `vmax <= 3.6 V` (S1-S6)
        *   `vpp <= 0.02 V` (S1-S6)
        *   `tup <= 0.15 s` (S1-S6)
        *   `dv <= 0.01 V` (S1-S6)
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source, $C_p = 25$ nF, $R_{leak} = 20$ M$\Omega$.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (nom), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong exc/light load), S4 (weak exc), S5 (low freq), S6 (hot/Cp+20%).
    *   Key Problem: "underpower" - previous designs (SECE variants) failed to deliver enough power to keep `vout >= 1.8 V`.
    *   Current Best: `SSHI_FBR_Zener`. It passed S3 but failed almost everything else because the average output voltage was too low (1.18V for S1, 1.00V for S2, 0.69V for S4).

    *   The `SSHI_FBR_Zener` (topology 40eae91a637a) uses a combination of an SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) stage and a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR).
    *   Wait, look at the `SSHI_FBR_Zener` components:
        `L1 pzp n1`, `S1 n1 pzn`, `G1 SYNC`, `D1 pzp out`, `D2 pzn out`, `D3 0 pzp`, `D4 0 pzn`.
        This is effectively a piezo in parallel with an inductor/switch (SSHI) and a full bridge rectifier.
        The SSHI part (L1, S1) helps flip the voltage on $C_p$ to increase extracted energy.
        The bridge (D1-D4) converts the AC piezo voltage to DC at `out`.
    *   Why did it fail `vout_min`?
        Even with SSHI, the voltage magnitude of the piezo might not be high enough to push enough current through the bridge diodes to overcome the load current, especially for S2 and S4.
        Wait, the bridge diodes are DSCH (~0.25V drop).
        The open-circuit voltage of the piezo is $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$.
        For S1: $50\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
        With a full bridge, you lose $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$.
        $3.18 - 0.5 = 2.68\text{V}$. The output should be able to reach 1.8V.
        But the SSHI is designed to flip the voltage. If the flipping isn't efficient or the timing is wrong, the energy extraction is poor.
        Actually, the `SSHI_FBR_Zener` failed `vout_min` because the average output was only 1.18V (S1) and 1.00V (S2). This suggests the bridge rectifier might be limiting the current or the SSHI isn't providing enough boost.

    *   Full Bridge Rectifiers (FBR) are simple but have a high voltage drop (2 diodes).
    *   Half-wave rectifiers are worse.
    *   Synchronous Rectification (using switches instead of diodes) reduces the drop to $I \cdot R_{on}$.
    *   SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) is usually more efficient than SSHI for certain conditions.
    *   Wait, the prompt says the last three designs (SECE variants) all failed the screen due to "underpower". This is a huge hint. Let's look at why SECE might underpower. SECE usually uses a switch and a diode (or two). If the switch is not timed correctly or the storage cap is too small, it fails.
    *   Let's look at the "Symmetric SECE" that failed the screen: `S1 pzp n1`, `S2 pzn n1`, `L1 n1 n2`, `D1 n2 out`. This is a weird topology.

    *   A classic SSHI circuit (standard) doesn't use a full bridge. It uses a half-bridge or a specific rectifier.
    *   Actually, the most efficient interface for a piezo is often a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) circuit with a *half-bridge* or a simple diode-capacitor rectifier if the voltage is high enough.
    *   But we need to be robust across S1-S6.
    *   Let's try a *synchronous* full-bridge or a synchronous rectifier. But we are limited to 4 switches.
    *   A full bridge requires 4 switches. If we use all 4 for rectification, we have no switches left for SSHI/SECE.
    *   What about an SSHI with a *half-bridge* (using 2 switches for rectification and 1 for the flipping)?
        Actually, a common high-efficiency SSHI uses a diode-bridge and an inductor-switch in parallel with the piezo.
        Wait, the `SSHI_FBR_Zener` (topology 40eae91a637a) *is* exactly that. Why did it fail?
        Maybe the inductor L1 was too large or the ton was wrong? No, the system optimizes those.
        Maybe the bridge diodes (DSCH) are still too restrictive?
        Wait, the `vavg` was 1.18V for S1. The open circuit voltage is 3.18V. The bridge drop is 0.5V. So we have 2.68V available. If the output is only 1.18V, it means the inductor-switch part is *consuming* power or not helping.

    *   The "underpower" for SECE suggests the energy extraction is too low.
    *   The "underpower" for SSHI_FBR suggests the rectified voltage is too low.
    *   Let's try a different approach: **Active Rectification (Synchronous Rectification)**.
    *   A synchronous rectifier using 2 switches (half-wave) or 4 switches (full-wave).
    *   If we use 4 switches for a full bridge:
        S1: pzp -> out
        S2: pzn -> out
        S3: 0 -> pzp
        S4: 0 -> pzn
        But we need a controller. A SYNC controller can only trigger switches at the extrema.
        If we have 4 switches, we can have 2 SYNCs.
        G1: edges=both, phase=0 (triggers S1 and S3)
        G2: edges=both, phase=0.5 (triggers S2 and S4) -- wait, phase is -0.25 to 0.25.
        Wait, the SYNC controller triggers at "piezo voltage extrema".
        Extrema occur every half period.
        If `edges="both"`, it triggers at both peaks.
        If we use two SYNCs:
        G1: edges="pos", phase=0 (positive peak)
        G2: edges="neg", phase=0 (negative peak)
        At positive peak:
        Piezo voltage $V_{pzp}$ is max, $V_{pzn}$ is min.
        We want to connect $pzp \to out$ and $pzn \to 0$.
        At negative peak:
        Piezo voltage $V_{pzp}$ is min, $V_{pzn}$ is max.
        We want to connect $pzn \to out$ and $pzp \to 0$.

    *   This is essentially a synchronous bridge. Let's try this.
        Wait, the SYNC controller "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds".
        If the switch is only closed for a few microseconds (ton), it's not a rectifier; it's a switched-capacitor converter!
        The SYNC controller is *not* a "keep-on until next edge" switch. It's a pulse.
        This means the SYNC controller is designed for SSHI or SECE, not for continuous rectification.

    *   If we can't use SYNC for continuous rectification, we must use diodes for the main path and SYNC for the "energy boost" (like SSHI).
    *   Why did `SSHI_FBR_Zener` fail?
        `S1 n1 pzn`, `L1 pzp n1`.
        This is an SSHI inductor flip. When S1 closes, the current in L1 (which was building up) flows, flipping the charge on $C_p$.
        But the bridge (D1-D4) is always there.
        Wait, if the bridge is always there, the $C_p$ is clamped to $V_{out} \pm V_{diode}$.
        If $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$, then $V_{pzp}$ is clamped between $1.8 - 0.25 = 1.55\text{V}$ and $1.8 + 0.25 = 2.05\text{V}$ (approximately).
        The SSHI inductor flip only works if the voltage can swing. If the bridge clamps the voltage, the inductor can't store much energy.
        *Crucial Insight:* For SSHI to work, the rectifier must be *disconnected* during the flip, or the flip must happen at the peaks where the diodes are already conducting.
        But in `SSHI_FBR_Zener`, the inductor is in parallel with the piezo. When S1 closes, the loop is $pzp \to L1 \to n1 \to S1 \to pzn \to pzp$.
        The bridge diodes are also connected to $pzp$ and $pzn$.
        If $V_{out}$ is 1.8V, the bridge diodes (D1-D4) will constrain the voltage of $pzp$ and $pzn$.
        Specifically, D1 (pzp $\to$ out) and D3 (0 $\to$ pzp) clamp $pzp$ between $V_{out}-0.25$ and $V_{out}+0.25$.
        This prevents the piezo voltage from reaching its full $V_{oc}$ (3.18V), which in turn limits the energy the inductor can store and flip.

    *   To fix this, we need a way to extract energy *without* clamping the piezo voltage too early, or use a topology that doesn't rely on a full bridge.
    *   Let's try SECE again, but *correctly*.
        SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) works by:
        1.  Letting $C_p$ charge up to its peak $V_{oc}$.
        2.  At the peak, closing a switch to connect $C_p$ to an inductor $L$ and a diode $D$ leading to $C_{out}$.
        3.  The energy is transferred from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ via the LC resonant circuit.
    *   SECE Topology:
        `S1` connects `pzp` to `n1`.
        `L1` connects `n1` to `n2`.
        `D1` connects `n2` to `out`.
        `G1` controls `S1`, `edges="both"` (or `pos`/`neg`).
        Wait, this only extracts energy from one polarity.
        For both polarities:
        S1 (pzp $\to$ n1) and S2 (pzn $\to$ n1).
        G1 (pos peak) triggers S1, G2 (neg peak) triggers S2.
        Wait, if we have S1 and S2 both going to `n1`, then:
        `S1: pzp, n1`
        `S2: pzn, n1`
        `L1: n1, n2`
        `D1: n2, out`
        At positive peak: $V_{pzp}$ is high, $V_{pzn}$ is low. S1 closes, $C_p$ discharges through L1 and D1 to `out`.
        At negative peak: $V_{pzn}$ is high (relative to 0, but $V_{pzp}$ is low). Wait, if S2 closes, $V_{pzn}$ is negative. $V_{pzn} \to n1 \to L1 \to D1 \to out$.
        This won't work because $V_{pzn}$ is negative at the negative peak.
        To extract from the negative peak, we need the current to flow *from* the piezo.
        At negative peak, $V_{pzn}$ is $-3.18\text{V}$ and $V_{pzp}$ is $+3.18\text{V}$.
        Wait, the piezo is a *current source*.
        $I_{piezo} = I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
        Voltage $V_{pzp}$ is the integral of $I_{piezo}/C_p$.
        $V_{pzp}(t) = -\frac{I_p}{\omega C_p} \cos(\omega t)$.
        Positive peak of $V_{pzp}$ is at $\omega t = \pi$ (where $\sin(\omega t) = 0$).
        At $\omega t = \pi$, $V_{pzp} = +3.18\text{V}, V_{pzn} = -3.18\text{V}$.
        At $\omega t = 2\pi$, $V_{pzp} = -3.18\text{V}, V_{pzn} = +3.18\text{V}$.

        So:
        Positive peak of $V_{pzp}$: Connect $pzp \to n1 \to L1 \to D1 \to out$.
        Negative peak of $V_{pzp}$: Connect $pzn \to n1 \to L1 \to D1 \to out$.
        This *does* work! Both peaks transfer energy to `out`.

    *   Now, let's refine the components:
        - S1: `pzp`, `n1`, ctrl=G1 (edges="pos", phase=0)
        - S2: `pzn`, `n1`, ctrl=G2 (edges="neg", phase=0)
        - L1: `n1`, `n2`
        - D1: `n2`, `out` (DSCH)
        - C_out: `out`, `0`
        - DZ1: `0`, `out` (Zener clamp to 3.3V)
        - G1: SYNC, ton=... (needs to be $\approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$), phase=0, edges="pos"
        - G2: SYNC, ton=... (needs to be $\approx \pi\sqrt{LC_p}$), phase=0, edges="neg"

    *   Is this what the "Symmetric_SECE" was?
        Symmetric_SECE: `S1 pzp n1 ctrl=G1`, `S2 pzn n1 ctrl=G2`, `L1 n1 n2 0.002`, `D1 n2 out DSCH`, `G1 SYNC ton=2e-05s phase=0 edges=pos`, `G2 SYNC ton=2e-05s phase=0 edges=neg`, `Cout out 0 4.7e-06`, `DZ1 0 out DZ33`.
        YES, it is. And it failed the screen with -8%, -56%, -18%.
        Wait, why did it fail the screen?
        Screening is done with `out` fixed at 1.8V.
        The net power delivered is measured.
        If it's -8%, it means it's *consuming* power.
        How can a SECE circuit consume power?
        The only way is if the SYNC controller's 0.5 uA supply current is larger than the harvested power, or if the switches are creating a path to ground.
        But there is no path to ground except through the load RL (which is replaced by 1.8V in screen).
        Wait, the SYNC controller's power cost is 0.5 uA.
        At 1.8V, $P_{sync} = 1.8\text{V} \times 0.5\mu\text{A} = 0.9\mu\text{W}$.
        If the harvested power is less than 0.9 uW, the net power is negative.
        This means the SECE circuit was harvesting almost *nothing*.

    *   Why would SECE harvest nothing?
        1.  `ton` is too small. (But the system optimizes `ton`).
        2.  `L1` is too large/small. (But the system optimizes `L1`).
        3.  The switches S1 and S2 are not closing at the right time.
        4.  The diode D1 is blocking the current.

        Wait, look at the `ton` in the failed Symmetric_SECE: `2e-05s`.
        For $L = 2\text{mH}$ and $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $\pi\sqrt{LC_p} = \pi\sqrt{2\cdot 10^{-3} \cdot 25\cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi\sqrt{5\cdot 10^{-11}} \approx 2.2\cdot 10^{-5}\text{s}$.
        The `ton` is $2\cdot 10^{-5}\text{s}$, which is very close.
        So why the failure?
        Maybe the "fixed 1.8V" during screening is the problem?
        In a SECE circuit, the energy is transferred in a burst. If `out` is fixed at 1.8V, the diode D1 will only conduct if $V_{n2} > 1.8 + 0.25 = 2.05\text{V}$.
        With $V_{pzp} = 3.18\text{V}$, the peak voltage $V_{n2}$ can reach $2 \times V_{pzp} = 6.36\text{V}$ (in an ideal LC circuit).
        So it should definitely conduct.

    *   Let's reconsider the "underpower" problem. If SECE and SSHI are both failing, maybe we need a simpler but more robust approach?
        What about a **Voltage Doubler** (Dickson Charge Pump)?
        A piezo can be seen as an AC source. A voltage doubler could boost the voltage.
        But the current is very low.
